newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Treasury ponders bids for Banco di Napoli.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Treasury ponders bids for Banco di Napoli.

text.p: The Italian Treasury faces an awkward choice between two largely state-owned groupings to decide who will win control of loss-making Banco di Napoli, banking analysts said on Friday.

The Treasury's bid deadline for a 60 percent stake in the ailing southern Italian bank closes on Friday with only two definite offers declared and no sign of a rich north Italian or north European banking group riding to the rescue.
"It looks likely that the Treasury will have to choose between two of its own banks, which puts it in a rather embarrassing position," said one banking analyst in Milan.

The European Commission is clearly unhappy at the Italian government's efforts to bail out Italy's record loss-making bank which may still keep it largely in state hands and could be interpreted as a disguised form of national state aid.

On Thursday, Italy's Banca Nazionale del Lavoro (BNL) confirmed it had decided along with insurer INA to make a joint offer for Banco di Napoli, as did state-owned credit institute Mediocredito Centrale.

But with BNL 85-percent and INA 34-percent Treasury-owned, and Mediocredito completely in the hands of the Treasury, hope of a rescue for southern Italy's largest bank by an independent banking group has worn thin.

The war of words between Italy and the Commission seemed to ease on Friday when the Commission said it had been assured that Italy would take the necessary measures to enable the European Union to clear a capital injection of two trillion lire ($1.3 billion) before the stake sell-off.

But EU rules ban state subsidies to businesses unless accompanied by strict restructuring plans to ensure their long-term viability, and analysts said it was not clear the Banco di Napoli plan would completely satisfy the Commission.

Earlier this week, European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert expressed "astonishment" at Italy's decision to go ahead with the capital issue, adding to worries about a Treasury-controlled bank taking over Banco di Napoli.

In mid-November, Banco di Napoli said three Italian and three foreign institutions had expressed interest, But while the three Italian names became known, there have been few clues to the identities of the overseas institutions.

In fact, Banco di Napoli's chairman Guiseppe Falcone and director general Federico Pepe have suggested a three-way bid between all three interested Italian partners would make a very competitive combination.

Banco di Napoli unveiled a loss of 3.12 trillion lire ($2 billion) for 1995, the largest loss in Italian banking history, and plunged a further 674 billion lire into the red in the first half of 1996.
Analysts still have many doubts over a rescue attempt for the Naples-based bank with its history of poor loan management, high labour costs and unwieldy management structure.
"Since there appears little concrete interest in the bank from other groups, it would appear the Treasury will be forced to keep it in quasi-state hands," said another Milan analyst. ($1=1,530 lire)
